q: An enterprise borrows Rs 5,00,000 at 10% per annum, repayable in equal annual instalments of Rs 2,01,060. Of the first instalment paid at the end of Year 1, the amount that goes towards repayment of the principal is:
e: Interest in first instalment = 10 percent x Rs 5,00,000 = Rs 50,000. Principal repaid = Rs 2,01,060 - Rs 50,000 = Rs 1,51,060.

q: The cost of raising fresh equity share capital is ordinarily higher than the cost of retained earnings of the same company, mainly because:

options.A: Retained earnings carry a legal obligation to pay dividends
options.B: Fresh equity shares rank after retained earnings for repayment
options.C: Retained earnings are taxed at a higher rate in the company's hands
options.D: A fresh issue involves flotation costs such as brokerage and issue expenses, which retained earnings do not

e: A fresh equity issue involves flotation costs like brokerage and issue expenses, reducing net proceeds and raising its cost. Retained earnings involve no such costs, so fresh equity ordinarily costs more.

q: On the Capital Asset Pricing Model, the cost of equity capital of a company works out to 16% per annum. The risk-free rate is 6% per annum and the expected return on the market portfolio is 14% per annum. The beta of the company's share is:
In arriving at the initial cash outlay of a project to acquire and install a new plant, which of the following is correctly included?

options.A: The cost of the plant together with freight, installation and trial-run expenses incurred to bring it into working condition
options.B: A share of the existing head-office establishment expenses apportioned to the plant
options.C: The market value of a different plant already owned and used elsewhere in the factory
options.D: The interest paid on a loan taken after the plant has been commissioned

e: Initial outlay includes the plant cost together with freight, installation and trial-run expenses to bring it into working condition, as all are necessary to make the asset ready for use. Apportioned head-office costs and later loan interest are excluded.

q: A machine has an Equivalent Annual Cost of Rs 1,60,000. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the discount rate used is 3.170. The present value of all the costs of owning and operating the machine over its life is:
e: PV of all costs = Equivalent Annual Cost x Annuity factor = Rs 1,60,000 x 3.170 = Rs 5,07,200.

q: Where an enterprise has ample funds and a set of independent projects is under consideration, the correct acceptance rule under the Net Present Value method is to:

options.A: Accept only the single project with the highest Net Present Value
options.B: Accept the projects in the order of their internal rates of return until the best one is exhausted
options.C: Reject all projects whose payback period exceeds the average life of the set
options.D: Accept every project that shows a positive Net Present Value

e: With ample funds and independent projects, NPV rule is to accept every project with positive NPV, as each adds to wealth and none competes with another for funds.

q: The free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) of an enterprise for a year is Rs 9,20,000. During the year it paid interest of Rs 1,50,000, the tax rate being 30%, and it raised fresh borrowings exceeding its repayments by Rs 80,000. The free cash flow to equity (FCFE) is:
The marginal cost of capital of an enterprise, as distinct from its average cost of capital, generally rises as larger and larger amounts of fresh capital are raised in a period, mainly because:

options.A: The average cost of capital is computed only on the existing capital
options.B: Additional capital must be drawn from progressively more expensive sources and on less favourable terms as the cheaper sources are used up
options.C: Fresh capital is always raised only in the form of equity shares
options.D: The cost of retained earnings rises with every increase in the dividend rate

e: Marginal cost of capital rises as more capital is raised because additional capital must come from progressively more expensive sources on less favourable terms once cheaper sources are used up.

q: The financial (market-price) cost of a component of a public project is Rs 8,00,000. The standard conversion factor applicable to such costs is 0.85. In the economic appraisal of the project, the component will be taken at:
e: Economic (shadow) value = Financial cost x Standard conversion factor = Rs 8,00,000 x 0.85 = Rs 6,80,000.

q: In estimating the terminal (continuing) value of a project on the assumption that its cash flows will grow at a constant rate indefinitely after the forecast period, a condition that must hold for the estimate to be meaningful is that:

options.A: The assumed growth rate must exceed the discount rate
options.B: The assumed growth rate must be equal to the discount rate
options.C: The cash flows must stop growing after a fixed number of years
options.D: The assumed growth rate must remain below the discount rate

e: In the constant-growth terminal value formula, value = Cash flow / (discount rate - growth rate). It is meaningful only if the growth rate remains below the discount rate, otherwise the denominator is zero or negative.

q: Even where a project's physical volume of business is expected to remain constant, rising prices over its life will ordinarily require additional investment in working capital in later years, because:

options.A: The same physical quantities of stock and receivables must be carried at higher money values
options.B: Depreciation charged each year increases with the price level
options.C: Creditors allow longer credit when prices rise
options.D: Working capital is recovered only at the end of the project's life

e: With constant physical volume, higher prices mean the same quantities of stock and receivables are carried at higher money values. Additional working capital investment is therefore needed in later years despite unchanged volume.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 14,40,000 and its inventory turnover ratio is 6 times. Its closing inventory is Rs 2,80,000. Its opening inventory was:
e: Average inventory = COGS / Turnover = Rs 14,40,000 / 6 = Rs 2,40,000. Average = (Opening + 2,80,000) / 2 = 2,40,000, so Opening = 4,80,000 - 2,80,000 = Rs 2,00,000.

q: A company makes extensive use of assets held under operating leases, the obligations under which do not appear as debt in its balance sheet. The main caution in reading its debt-equity ratio is that the ratio:

options.A: Overstates the company's leverage because lease rentals are treated as debt
options.B: Cannot be computed at all for a company that leases assets
options.C: Understates the company's true fixed obligations, since the committed lease payments are left out of the debt figure
options.D: Is unaffected, because lease obligations are always negligible

e: Operating lease obligations do not appear as debt in the balance sheet, yet lease payments are committed fixed obligations. The debt-equity ratio therefore understates true fixed obligations and leverage.

q: The debtors turnover ratio of an enterprise is 5 times and its average trade debtors are Rs 3,60,000. Its net credit sales for the year were:
e: Net credit sales = Debtors turnover x Average debtors = 5 x Rs 3,60,000 = Rs 18,00,000.

q: The quick ratio and the current ratio of a service enterprise, such as a transport or consultancy undertaking, are ordinarily close to each other, mainly because:

options.A: Such an enterprise holds little or no stock, so there is little to exclude in arriving at liquid assets
options.B: Such an enterprise has no current liabilities
options.C: Its debtors are always collected within a few days
options.D: Its current assets consist wholly of cash and bank balances

e: Quick assets are current assets minus stock. A service enterprise holds little or no stock, so little is excluded and its quick ratio stays ordinarily close to its current ratio.

q: The excess of the current assets of an enterprise over its current liabilities is Rs 4,20,000, and its current liabilities amount to Rs 3,80,000. The amount of its current assets is:
e: Working capital (CA - CL) = Rs 4,20,000 and CL = Rs 3,80,000, so Current assets = 4,20,000 + 3,80,000 = Rs 8,00,000.

q: An inventory turnover ratio that is exceptionally high, well above that of comparable enterprises, is not necessarily a sign of good inventory management, because it may indicate that:

options.A: The enterprise is holding stock of very high value
options.B: The cost of goods sold has been understated in the accounts
options.C: Stocks are kept so low that the enterprise risks stock-outs and lost sales
options.D: The enterprise sells mostly for cash rather than on credit

e: An exceptionally high inventory turnover may mean stocks are kept so low that the enterprise risks stock-outs and lost sales. It is not necessarily a sign of good inventory management.

q: The debt-equity ratio (long-term debt to shareholders' funds) of an enterprise is 0.75 : 1 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 16,00,000. Its long-term debt is:
e: Long-term debt = Debt-equity ratio x Shareholders funds = 0.75 x Rs 16,00,000 = Rs 12,00,000.

q: A company has cumulative preference shares outstanding. For computing its Earnings Per Share, the preference dividend for the year is deducted from the profit after tax:

options.A: Only if the dividend has actually been declared by the company
options.B: Only if the dividend has actually been paid during the year
options.C: Only when the company has accumulated profits of earlier years
options.D: Whether or not it has been declared, since the cumulative dividend accrues for the year in any case

e: For cumulative preference shares the dividend accrues for the year whether declared or not. For EPS it is deducted from profit after tax in every case; for non-cumulative shares deduction depends on declaration.

q: The profit available for equity shareholders of a company is Rs 12,00,000 and it has 3,00,000 equity shares. The company buys back 60,000 of its shares, the profit available remaining unchanged. Its Earnings Per Share after the buy-back will be:

An enterprise has large contingent liabilities, such as guarantees given and bills discounted, which are disclosed only as footnotes to its balance sheet. In judging its solvency from the balance sheet ratios, the analyst should bear in mind that:

options.A: The solvency ratios flatter the enterprise, because these possible obligations form no part of the liabilities used in the ratios
options.B: Contingent liabilities are already included in the total debt of the enterprise
options.C: Contingent liabilities have no bearing on solvency in any circumstance
options.D: The current ratio alone fully captures the effect of contingent liabilities

e: Contingent liabilities like guarantees and bills discounted appear only as footnotes and form no part of liabilities used in solvency ratios. The ratios therefore flatter the enterprise solvency.

q: The average inventory of an enterprise is Rs 3,65,000 and it is held, on average, for 73 days of a 365-day year. The cost of goods sold for the year is:
e: Inventory holding = Average inventory / COGS x 365 = 73 days, so COGS = Rs 3,65,000 x 365 / 73 = Rs 18,25,000.

q: Diluted Earnings Per Share is computed and reported by a company in addition to its basic Earnings Per Share in order to show:

options.A: The earnings per share after providing for all unpaid preference dividends of past years
options.B: The fall in earnings per share that would occur if convertible securities and similar rights were converted into equity shares, increasing the number of shares
options.C: The earnings per share after deducting the proposed dividend from the profit
options.D: The earnings per share restated at constant prices for the effect of inflation

e: Diluted EPS shows the fall in EPS that would occur if convertible securities and similar rights were converted into equity shares, increasing the number of shares among which earnings are spread.

q: The capital gearing ratio of a company, reckoned as the ratio of its fixed-cost capital (preference capital and debentures) to its equity share capital, is 1.5 : 1. Its fixed-cost capital amounts to Rs 15,00,000. Its equity share capital is:
e: Equity share capital = Fixed-cost capital / Gearing ratio = Rs 15,00,000 / 1.5 = Rs 10,00,000.

q: The market price of a company's share ordinarily stands well above its book value per share, mainly because:

options.A: The book value per share records the assets at their historical cost and leaves out the earning capacity and unrecorded intangibles, such as goodwill, on which the market value rests
options.B: The book value per share is computed after deducting the market price of the share
options.C: Companies are required to state their assets below their realisable value in all cases
options.D: The number of shares used in computing book value is larger than the number actually issued

e: Market price rests on earning capacity and unrecorded intangibles like goodwill. Book value records assets at historical cost and leaves these out, so market price ordinarily stands well above book value per share.

q: The net profit ratio of an enterprise is 12% and its net profit after tax for the year is Rs 2,16,000. Its net sales for the year were:
e: Net sales = Net profit / Net profit ratio = Rs 2,16,000 / 0.12 = Rs 18,00,000.

q: For appraising the creditworthiness of a borrowing enterprise, lenders commonly work out its tangible net worth by deducting intangible assets such as goodwill, patents carried at unamortised cost and preliminary expenses from its net worth. This is done because:

options.A: Intangible assets are not recorded in the books of account at all
options.B: Such assets ordinarily have little or no realisable value for the lender if the enterprise has to be wound up
options.C: Intangible assets are always valued above their cost in the balance sheet
options.D: The Companies Act requires net worth to be stated only on this basis

e: Tangible net worth excludes intangible assets because goodwill, unamortised patents and preliminary expenses ordinarily have little or no realisable value for a lender if the enterprise is wound up.

q: On the DuPont decomposition, an enterprise has a Return on Equity of 24% and a Return on Assets of 8%. Its equity multiplier (total assets divided by equity funds) is:

options.A: 2 times
options.B: 3 times
options.C: 4 times
options.D: 1.5 times

e: On DuPont, ROE = ROA x Equity multiplier, so Equity multiplier = 24 / 8 = 3 times.

q: The current ratio of an enterprise may overstate its real ability to meet its current liabilities when:

options.A: A large part of its trade debtors consists of long-overdue debts of doubtful recovery, taken into current assets at their full book value
options.B: Its current assets include a large cash and bank balance
options.C: Its stock is valued on the first-in, first-out basis
options.D: Its current liabilities include a bank overdraft repayable on demand

e: If a large part of debtors consists of long-overdue debts of doubtful recovery taken at full book value, current assets are overstated. The current ratio then overstates real ability to meet current liabilities.

q: The selling and distribution expenses of an enterprise are Rs 1,44,000, and they work out to 9% of its net sales. Its net sales are:
e: Net sales = Selling and distribution expenses / Percent of sales = Rs 1,44,000 / 0.09 = Rs 16,00,000.

q: A known limitation of the interest coverage ratio as a measure of an enterprise's safety is that it takes no account of:

options.A: The tax payable on the profits of the enterprise
options.B: The depreciation charged on the fixed assets
options.C: The obligation to repay the principal of the loans as the instalments fall due, which must also be met out of earnings and cash flows
options.D: The preference dividend payable by the enterprise

e: Interest coverage compares earnings with interest only. It takes no account of the obligation to repay loan principal as instalments fall due, which must also be met from earnings and cash flows.

q: Trend percentages computed for the sales and profits of an enterprise become misleading or meaningless when:

options.A: The base year figures are taken from the audited accounts
options.B: The base year happens to be a year of loss, so that the base figure is negative and percentages computed on it convey no useful meaning
options.C: The period covered by the trend is longer than five years
options.D: The enterprise has changed its financial year during the period

e: Trend percentages need a positive, normal base. If the base year is a loss year, the base figure is negative and percentages computed on it are misleading or meaningless.

q: On the DuPont decomposition, an enterprise raises its Return on Equity from one year to the next purely by increasing its equity multiplier, its profit margin and assets turnover remaining unchanged. The correct reading of this improvement is that:

options.A: The enterprise has become more profitable in its operations
options.B: Its operating efficiency has improved in the same proportion
options.C: The higher return has been obtained by employing more debt in proportion to equity, and therefore carries higher financial risk rather than any operating improvement
options.D: Its total assets must have been reduced during the year

e: Raising ROE only by increasing the equity multiplier, with margin and turnover unchanged, means more debt relative to equity. The higher return carries higher financial risk, not any operating improvement.

q: The shareholders' funds of a company are such that its Return on Equity works out to 20%, the profit after tax being Rs 6,00,000. The shareholders' funds are:
e: Shareholders funds = Profit after tax / ROE = Rs 6,00,000 / 0.20 = Rs 30,00,000.

q: An enterprise that follows a policy of low profit margins but very rapid turnover of its assets may still earn a satisfactory Return on Assets, because the return is the product of the margin and the turnover. This illustrates that:

options.A: Profit margin alone is a complete measure of profitability
options.B: A low margin is always preferable to a high margin
options.C: Turnover of assets has no bearing on the return earned on them
options.D: Profitability must be judged by considering the margin on sales and the turnover of assets together, neither being conclusive by itself

e: Return on Assets is the product of profit margin and assets turnover. Low margin with very rapid turnover can still give satisfactory return, so margin and turnover must be judged together.

q: Under the Delphi technique of forecasting sales for the sales budget, the forecast is arrived at by:

options.A: Taking the arithmetic average of the sales of the last five years without any adjustment
options.B: Obtaining the considered estimates of a panel of experts through successive rounds of anonymous questionnaires, the summary of each round being fed back to the panel, until their views converge towards a consensus
options.C: Asking each salesman to estimate the sales of his own territory and simply adding up the estimates so received
options.D: Engaging a single outside consultant whose forecast is accepted without question

e: Under Delphi, a panel of experts gives estimates through successive rounds of anonymous questionnaires, with each round summary fed back, until views converge towards a consensus forecast.

q: The appropriation budget of an enterprise, which forms a part of its master budget, primarily shows:

options.A: The quantity of finished goods proposed to be produced during the budget period
options.B: The cash expected to be received from the debtors of the enterprise during the budget period
options.C: The manner in which the budgeted net profit of the period is proposed to be dealt with, that is, the provision proposed for taxation, the dividends proposed to be paid and the amounts proposed to be transferred to reserves
options.D: The capital expenditure proposed to be incurred on the plant and machinery of the enterprise

e: The appropriation budget shows how budgeted net profit will be dealt with - provision for taxation, dividends proposed and amounts transferred to reserves. It forms part of the master budget.

q: The cash budget of an enterprise is ordinarily prepared after the other functional budgets have been prepared, mainly because:

options.A: It merely brings together, in terms of the periods in which cash will actually be received and paid, the cash effects of the sales, purchases, wages, overhead and capital expenditure budgets
options.B: The cash budget is of no use until the actual results of the year are known
options.C: Cash transactions are too few in number to require an early budget
options.D: The law requires the cash budget to be the last document to be prepared

e: The cash budget is prepared after other functional budgets because it brings together, by period of actual receipt and payment, the cash effects of the sales, purchases, wages, overhead and capital expenditure budgets.

q: A material price variance has been reported for a department. In the ordinary course, the responsibility for this variance rests primarily on:

options.A: The production manager, because he supervises the workers who handle the material
options.B: The stores manager, because he is the custodian of the material in the stores
options.C: The sales manager, because he fixes the selling price of the finished product
options.D: The purchase manager or the buying department, because the variance arises from paying prices for materials different from those standardised or budgeted for purchases

e: A material price variance arises from paying prices different from standard or budgeted purchase prices. Responsibility rests primarily on the purchase manager or buying department, not on production, stores or sales.

q: In the course of a single budget period of an enterprise, the factor that limits its activities may itself change, for example, demand may be the limiting factor in some months and the availability of a material or of plant capacity in others. The correct approach to budgeting in such a case is to:

options.A: Assume throughout the period the factor that was limiting at the commencement of the period
options.B: Recognise the factor that is expected to be operative during each part of the period and build the functional budgets for that part accordingly
options.C: Prepare the budgets without reference to any limiting factor at all
options.D: Postpone the preparation of the budgets until the factor stops changing

e: When the limiting factor changes within a budget period, the factor expected to be operative in each part of the period must be recognised and functional budgets for that part built accordingly.

q: The total sales volume variance of an enterprise can be analysed into a market size variance and a market share variance. The market share variance measures:

options.A: The effect on the budgeted contribution of the change in the enterprise's share of the total market, that is, the difference between its actual and budgeted market shares applied to the actual total market volume
options.B: The effect of the change in the total size of the market itself, assuming the enterprise retained its budgeted share of it
options.C: The effect of the change in the selling price of the product of the enterprise
options.D: The effect of the change in the variable cost per unit of the product

e: Market share variance measures the effect on budgeted contribution of the change in the enterprise share of the total market - the difference between actual and budgeted market shares applied to the actual total market volume.

q: For the effective control of capital expenditure, it is not sufficient to watch only the amounts actually paid out against a sanctioned project. It is equally necessary to watch the commitments entered into, that is, the orders placed, mainly because:

options.A: Orders placed can always be cancelled without any loss to the enterprise
options.B: The payments against a project are always made in the same month in which the orders are placed
options.C: Once an order is placed, the enterprise is bound to incur the expenditure in future, so that the total of the expenditure already incurred and the commitments outstanding shows whether the sanctioned amount is likely to be exceeded
options.D: Commitments are recorded only to help the stores department in planning its godown space

e: Once an order is placed the enterprise is bound to incur the expenditure in future. Watching incurred expenditure plus outstanding commitments shows whether the sanctioned capital amount is likely to be exceeded; watching payments alone is insufficient.

q: In preparing the production budget of an enterprise, the level of the closing stock of finished goods to be provided for is decided mainly with reference to:

options.A: The closing stock that happened to be held at the end of the previous year
options.B: The personal preference of the production manager
options.C: The amount of the bank balance of the enterprise
options.D: The maximum and minimum stock levels laid down under the stock policy of the management, so that sales are not lost for want of stock and, at the same time, funds are not locked up in excessive stock

e: Closing finished goods stock in the production budget is decided with reference to maximum and minimum stock levels under management stock policy, balancing lost sales against funds locked in excessive stock.

q: In the terminology in common use in the United States of America, the master budget of a business enterprise is often called its:

options.A: Profit plan, because it projects, in summary form, the planned profit and the planned financial position of the enterprise for the budget period
options.B: Cost plan, because it deals only with the costs of production
options.C: Cash plan, because it contains only the receipts and payments of cash
options.D: Works plan, because it is prepared only by the works department

e: In United States terminology the master budget is often called the profit plan, because it projects in summary form the planned profit and planned financial position for the budget period.

q: 'Pseudo-participation' in budgeting means a situation in which:

options.A: The subordinate managers themselves prepare the whole budget without any guidance from above
options.B: The subordinate managers are formally consulted and invited to give their views, but their views are in fact ignored and the targets are effectively imposed on them, so that the exercise breeds the same resentment and lack of commitment as a purely imposed budget
options.C: The budget is prepared jointly by the management and the external auditors of the enterprise
options.D: Participation in budgeting is confined to the shareholders of the enterprise

e: Pseudo-participation is formal consultation in which subordinate views are in fact ignored and targets effectively imposed. It breeds the same resentment and lack of commitment as a purely imposed budget.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 90,000, variable costs of Rs 8 per unit and a semi-variable cost consisting of a fixed element of Rs 24,000 plus Rs 3 per unit. The total flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 18,000 units is:

An enterprise orders plant costing Rs 9,00,000 on terms that 30% of the price is payable with the order, 50% on delivery and the balance of 20% one year after delivery. The order is placed and the delivery is taken during the current year, and erection charges of Rs 60,000 are also paid in cash during the current year. The cash outflow on capital account in respect of this plant during the current year, as it will appear in the cash budget, is:
e: Cash paid in current year = 30 percent with order (Rs 2,70,000) + 50 percent on delivery (Rs 4,50,000) + erection Rs 60,000 = Rs 7,80,000. The 20 percent payable after one year is excluded.

q: The sales of an enterprise in the base year were 40,000 units at Rs 50 per unit. For the budget year, the sales volume is expected to increase by 10%, but the selling price is expected to be reduced by 5%. The budgeted sales value for the budget year is:
e: Budget volume = 40,000 x 1.10 = 44,000 units. Budget price = Rs 50 x 0.95 = Rs 47.50. Budgeted sales value = 44,000 x 47.50 = Rs 20,90,000.

q: The budgeted cost of production of an enterprise for a period is Rs 9,60,000. The stock of finished goods is valued at Rs 1,20,000 at the commencement of the period and is to be raised to Rs 1,50,000 at the end of the period. The budgeted cost of goods sold for the period is:
e: Cost of goods sold = Cost of production + Opening stock - Closing stock = Rs 9,60,000 + Rs 1,20,000 - Rs 1,50,000 = Rs 9,30,000.

q: Under the arrangement of converting the hard-core portion of a cash credit limit into a working capital term loan, the bank:

options.A: Writes off the hard-core portion of the borrowings of the enterprise
options.B: Converts the whole of the cash credit limit into equity shares of the enterprise
options.C: Separates that part of the borrowings which remains utilised practically throughout the year, representing the permanent blockage of funds in current assets, and treats it as a term loan repayable in instalments over an agreed period, the balance alone continuing as a fluctuating cash credit
options.D: Sanctions an additional cash credit limit equal to the hard-core portion

e: Under the hard-core arrangement the bank separates borrowings utilised practically throughout the year, representing permanent blockage in current assets, and treats them as a term loan repayable in instalments. Only the balance continues as fluctuating cash credit.

q: A borrower stores the goods purchased by him in a warehouse approved by the bank and pledges the warehouse receipt with the bank in order to obtain working capital finance. The significant feature of this arrangement, from the standpoint of the bank, is that:

options.A: The bank obtains control over the goods through the warehouse receipt, and the goods are released to the borrower only in lots and against payment, so that the advance remains covered by the stock throughout
options.B: The borrower is free to sell the whole of the stock without informing the bank
options.C: The warehouse receipt is a mere formality and gives the bank no right over the goods
options.D: The bank itself becomes the owner of the goods for all purposes, including their sale in the market

e: A warehouse receipt pledged with the bank gives the bank control over the stored goods as security; the goods are released to the borrower only in lots against payment, so the advance stays covered by stock throughout.

q: Trade credit is said to be extended on 'open account' when:

options.A: The buyer issues post-dated cheques for the full value of every purchase
options.B: The buyer accepts a bill of exchange drawn on him by the seller for every consignment
options.C: The goods are supplied only against a bank guarantee furnished by the buyer
options.D: The seller ships the goods and sends the invoice, and the buyer pays the amount by the date agreed upon, no bill, note or other formal instrument being signed by the buyer, the arrangement resting on his credit standing and past dealings

e: Trade credit on open account means goods are shipped with an invoice and the buyer pays by the agreed date, with no bill, note or other formal instrument signed; the arrangement rests on the buyer's credit standing and past dealings.

q: A contractor receives a mobilisation advance from the employer at the commencement of a work. This advance reduces the working capital which the contractor must himself provide for the work, mainly because:

options.A: The advance is a gift which the contractor is never required to repay
options.B: A part of his initial outlay on establishing the site, moving his plant and purchasing the first lots of materials is met out of the employer's funds, the advance being recovered gradually by deduction from his running bills as the work progresses
options.C: The advance exempts the contractor from providing any security deposit for the work
options.D: The advance is paid only after the whole work has been completed and measured

e: A mobilisation advance meets part of the contractor's initial site, plant movement and first material costs out of the employer's funds, so his own working capital need falls; it is not a gift, being recovered gradually from running bills.

q: The earnest money and security deposits which a contracting enterprise has lodged with its clients form a part of its working capital, mainly because:

options.A: Such deposits remain blocked with the clients, commonly until the work is completed and the defect liability period is over, so that the funds of the enterprise stand invested in them in the meantime, although they earn little or no return
options.B: Such deposits can be withdrawn by the enterprise on any day it likes
options.C: Such deposits are paid by the clients to the enterprise and not by the enterprise to the clients
options.D: Such deposits are a part of the fixed assets of the enterprise

e: Earnest money and security deposits are working capital because the enterprise's funds remain blocked with clients until completion and the defect liability period is over, earning little or no return in the meantime.

q: An enterprise replaces a short-term bank borrowing, which it has been renewing from year to year, by a long-term loan of the same amount, the cash position and the other assets and liabilities remaining unchanged. The effect of this refinancing on its net working capital is that:

options.A: The net working capital decreases, because a long-term loan carries a higher rate of interest
options.B: The net working capital remains unchanged, because the total liabilities remain the same
options.C: The net working capital increases, because the current liabilities fall by the amount refinanced while the current assets are unaffected
options.D: The gross working capital increases, but the net working capital falls

e: Replacing a short-term borrowing with a long-term loan leaves current assets unchanged but reduces current liabilities by the amount refinanced, so net working capital, current assets minus current liabilities, increases by that amount.

q: 'Special' working capital of an enterprise is the working capital which is required:

options.A: Throughout the year for carrying on the normal operations of the enterprise
options.B: Regularly every year during the busy season of the enterprise
options.C: As a permanent minimum investment in current assets
options.D: For meeting special or unforeseen needs outside the regular course of operations, such as carrying out a special advertisement campaign, facing a strike or a flood, or launching an altogether new line of business

e: Special working capital is required for special or unforeseen needs outside regular operations, such as a special advertisement campaign, a strike or flood, or launching a new line; regular and seasonal needs are not special working capital.

q: In the terminology of working capital, the gross concept is called the quantitative concept and the net concept is called the qualitative concept, because:

options.A: The gross concept deals with the quality of the management of the enterprise
options.B: The gross concept concerns merely the total amount invested in current assets, whereas the net concept indicates the manner in which that investment is financed, that is, the portion of the current assets which is financed from long-term sources
options.C: The net concept is concerned only with the quantity of the stock held by the enterprise
options.D: Both the concepts are concerned only with the quantity of the current assets

e: The gross concept is quantitative because it concerns only the total amount invested in current assets; the net concept is qualitative because it shows how that investment is financed, namely the portion financed from long-term sources.

q: Under the system of end-of-month (EOM) dating of credit sales, the credit terms offered to the buyers are that:

options.A: All the purchases made by a buyer during a calendar month are treated as payable at the end of the month next following, so that the credit period is reckoned from the end of the month of purchase and not from the date of each invoice
options.B: The buyer must pay for every invoice on the very day on which the goods are received by him
options.C: The buyer may pay at any time within the next five years
options.D: A cash discount is allowed on all payments made on the last day of the month

e: Under end-of-month dating, all purchases during a calendar month are treated as payable at the end of the following month, so the credit period is reckoned from the end of the purchase month, not from each invoice date.

q: A bank guarantee furnished by a bank on behalf of its customer differs from a letter of credit opened by it in that:

options.A: A guarantee involves an immediate payment of cash by the bank in every case
options.B: A letter of credit is never honoured by the bank that issues it
options.C: A guarantee is a contingent undertaking under which the bank is called upon to pay only if the customer defaults in performing the contract or in paying the amount guaranteed, whereas a letter of credit is a payment undertaking which is honoured against the stipulated documents in the ordinary course of the transaction
options.D: There is no difference at all between a bank guarantee and a letter of credit

e: A bank guarantee is contingent, payable only if the customer defaults, whereas a letter of credit is a payment undertaking honoured against the stipulated documents in the ordinary course of the transaction.

q: The sound policy in regard to the payment of the trade creditors of an enterprise is to pay them on the due date, that is, at the end of the credit period allowed, mainly because:

options.A: Payment long before the due date increases the profit of the enterprise
options.B: Payment on the due date makes the fullest use of the interest-free credit available without damaging the credit standing of the enterprise, whereas habitual delay beyond the due date may lead the suppliers to restrict supplies, raise their prices or withdraw credit altogether
options.C: Creditors always allow a cash discount for payment on the due date
options.D: Payment on the due date is compulsory under the Companies Act in all cases

e: Paying creditors on the due date uses the full interest-free credit period without damaging credit standing; habitual delay beyond the due date may lead suppliers to restrict supplies, raise prices or withdraw credit.

q: Under the combined ABC and VED matrix method of selective inventory control, the stores items are classified simultaneously by their annual consumption value and by their criticality, and the items that receive the closest control, the most careful estimation of requirements and the highest management attention are those which are:

options.A: Of low value and merely desirable in nature
options.B: Of high value but entirely non-critical in nature
options.C: Of low value and vital in nature only
options.D: At once high in annual consumption value and vital to production, the two classifications being combined so that neither value nor criticality is considered in isolation

e: In the combined ABC-VED matrix, control is based on both annual consumption value and criticality together; items that are both high value (A) and vital (V) therefore receive the closest control and highest management attention.

q: An enterprise gives the following annual estimates: consumption of raw materials Rs 18,00,000, and raw materials are stocked for 2 months; cost of production Rs 24,00,000, and the work-in-progress remains in process for half a month; cost of goods sold Rs 27,00,000, and finished goods are stocked for 1 month; credit sales Rs 36,00,000, and debtors are collected after one and a half months; a cash balance of Rs 50,000 is to be maintained. Materials are purchased on 1 month's credit (purchases being equal to the consumption) and outstanding expenses are Rs 75,000. Its net working capital requirement is:
e: Current assets: raw material 18,00,000 x 2/12 = 3,00,000, WIP 24,00,000 x 0.5/12 = 1,00,000, finished goods 27,00,000 x 1/12 = 2,25,000, debtors 36,00,000 x 1.5/12 = 4,50,000, cash 50,000; total 11,25,000. Current liabilities: creditors 18,00,000 x 1/12 = 1,50,000 plus outstanding expenses 75,000 = 2,25,000. Net working capital = 11,25,000 - 2,25,000 = Rs 9,00,000.

q: An enterprise makes credit purchases of Rs 12,00,000 during a year on terms of 2/10, net 30, that is, a cash discount of 2% for payment within 10 days, the full amount being otherwise payable in 30 days. It decides to borrow from its bank at 12% per annum the amount needed to pay each bill on the tenth day. Its net gain from this course for the year, being the discount earned less the interest payable for the 20 days for which the money is paid early, is:
e: Discount earned = 2% of 12,00,000 = Rs 24,000. Amount borrowed to pay early = 12,00,000 - 24,000 = 11,76,000; interest at 12% for 20 days on a 360-day year = 11,76,000 x 12% x 20/360 = Rs 7,840. Net gain = 24,000 - 7,840 = Rs 16,160.

q: The average stock held by an enterprise during a year is Rs 8,00,000, its closing stock being Rs 10,00,000. The carrying cost of inventory, comprising the cost of the funds locked up, storage, insurance and the risk of obsolescence, is estimated at 20% per annum of the average stock held. The annual carrying cost of its inventory is:
e: Annual carrying cost is charged on average stock, not closing stock: 20% x Rs 8,00,000 average stock = Rs 1,60,000.

q: For the purposes of the applicability of the Accounting Standards to non-company enterprises, an enterprise is placed in Level I, the level to which Accounting Standard 3 on cash flow statements applies in full, where, among other criteria:

options.A: Its turnover is less than Rs 1 crore in the preceding year
options.B: Its turnover (excluding other income) exceeded Rs 50 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year
options.C: It has no borrowings of any kind
options.D: It employs fewer than ten persons

e: For non-company enterprises, Level I, to which AS-3 applies in full, includes enterprises whose turnover excluding other income exceeded Rs 50 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.

q: Under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the operating activities of an enterprise comprise:

options.A: Only those activities which result in changes in the size of the capital of the enterprise
options.B: Its principal revenue-producing activities and also all those other activities of the enterprise which cannot be classified either as investing activities or as financing activities
options.C: Only the activities relating to the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets
options.D: Only the activities relating to the raising and repayment of borrowings

e: Under AS-3, operating activities are the enterprise's principal revenue-producing activities plus all other activities that are neither investing nor financing activities.

q: In the balance sheets of an enterprise, the trade debtors are shown at their gross amount, without deducting the provision for doubtful debts made against them. In the schedule of changes in working capital, the provision for doubtful debts should accordingly be:

options.A: Ignored altogether, since it is not a liability at all
options.B: Deducted from the funds from operations of the year
options.C: Treated as a current liability, so that an increase in the provision during the year is shown as an increase in the current liabilities
options.D: Treated as a long-term liability in all cases

e: When debtors are shown gross without deducting the provision for doubtful debts, consistency in the working capital schedule requires the provision to be treated as a current liability; an increase in it is an increase in current liabilities.

q: An enterprise acquires a machine under a finance lease, no payment being made at the time the lease is entered into. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, this transaction is dealt with by:

options.A: Showing the full value of the machine as a cash outflow under investing activities
options.B: Showing the full value of the machine as a cash inflow under financing activities
options.C: Showing the value of the machine partly under investing and partly under financing activities
options.D: Excluding it from the cash flow statement altogether, since no cash has moved, and disclosing it elsewhere in the financial statements as a significant non-cash investing and financing transaction

e: Acquiring a machine under a finance lease with no payment at inception involves no cash flow, so it is excluded from the cash flow statement and disclosed elsewhere as a significant non-cash investing and financing transaction.

q: In a cash flow statement prepared by the indirect method, the figure described as 'cash generated from operations' is arrived at:

options.A: After deducting the income-tax paid during the year
options.B: Before deducting the income-tax paid during the year, the tax paid being deducted thereafter from that figure in order to arrive at the net cash flow from operating activities
options.C: After adding the proceeds of the loans raised during the year
options.D: Without making any adjustment for the changes in the current assets and current liabilities

e: In the indirect method, cash generated from operations is struck before deducting income tax paid; the tax paid is then deducted from that figure to arrive at net cash flow from operating activities.

q: In a cash flow statement prepared by the indirect method, the interest paid during the year, which is to be presented under financing activities, is dealt with in computing the operating profit before working capital changes by:

options.A: Adding back the interest charged in the profit and loss account to the net profit before tax, the cash actually paid as interest being then shown under financing activities
options.B: Deducting the interest twice from the net profit before tax
options.C: Ignoring the interest altogether at both the stages
options.D: Showing the interest paid as an application in the fund flow statement instead

e: Interest to be shown under financing activities is first added back, as charged in the profit and loss account, to net profit before tax in computing operating profit before working capital changes; the cash interest actually paid is then shown under financing.

q: In preparing a cash flow statement by the indirect method, an enterprise finds that it has charged in its profit and loss account an unrealised exchange loss arising on the restatement of its foreign currency borrowings at the closing rate. The correct treatment of this loss is to:

options.A: Show it as a cash outflow under financing activities
options.B: Ignore it completely, since it does not affect the profit of the year
options.C: Add it back to the net profit before tax, since it is a non-cash item which has reduced the reported profit without any outflow of cash, an unrealised exchange gain being similarly deducted
options.D: Show it as a cash outflow under operating activities

e: An unrealised exchange loss on restating foreign currency borrowings is non-cash, so it is added back to net profit before tax in the indirect method; an unrealised exchange gain would similarly be deducted.

q: In a fund flow statement, the funds from operations are generally regarded as the most important internal source of funds, mainly because:

options.A: They are contributed by the shareholders of the enterprise
options.B: They are raised by borrowing from the banks
options.C: They are realised by selling the fixed assets of the enterprise
options.D: They are generated by the enterprise itself out of its own operations, year after year, without creating any obligation to outsiders and without reducing its assets

e: Funds from operations are the most important internal source because they are generated by the enterprise itself from its own operations year after year, without creating an obligation to outsiders or reducing its assets.

q: A manufacturing enterprise receives compensation from its insurers under a policy covering the loss of profits during the period for which its factory remained closed following a fire. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, this receipt is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities, because the compensation stands in the place of the trading profits which the enterprise would have earned from its operations
options.B: Investing activities, because the receipt arises out of a fire in the factory
options.C: Financing activities, because the amount is received from an outside agency
options.D: No activity at all, because an insurance receipt is not a cash flow

e: Insurance compensation for loss of profits replaces the trading profits the enterprise would have earned, so under AS-3 it is classified as a cash flow from operating activities.

q: The net profit of an enterprise for a year is Rs 1,80,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 45,000 and a loss of Rs 12,000 on the sale of plant, after making a transfer of Rs 30,000 to the general reserve, and after crediting a profit of Rs 20,000 on the sale of its investments. During the year, its stock increased by Rs 35,000, its bills receivable decreased by Rs 15,000, its creditors increased by Rs 18,000 and its outstanding expenses decreased by Rs 8,000. Its cash generated from operating activities, before deducting the income-tax paid, computed by the indirect method, is:
e: Operating profit before working capital changes = 1,80,000 + transfer to reserve 30,000 + depreciation 45,000 + loss on sale of plant 12,000 - profit on sale of investments 20,000 = 2,47,000. Working capital changes: - stock increase 35,000 + bills receivable decrease 15,000 + creditors increase 18,000 - outstanding expenses decrease 8,000 = -10,000. Cash generated = 2,47,000 - 10,000 = Rs 2,37,000.

q: During a year, the stock of an enterprise increased by Rs 40,000, its debtors decreased by Rs 25,000 and its cash balance increased by Rs 10,000. Its creditors increased by Rs 15,000, its bills payable decreased by Rs 5,000 and its outstanding expenses increased by Rs 8,000. As per the schedule of changes in working capital, the net change in its working capital during the year is:

options.A: A decrease of Rs 7,000
options.B: An increase of Rs 25,000
options.C: An increase of Rs 43,000
options.D: An increase of Rs 7,000

e: Current assets change: stock +40,000 - debtors 25,000 + cash 10,000 = +25,000. Current liabilities change: creditors +15,000 - bills payable 5,000 + outstanding expenses 8,000 = +18,000. Net working capital change = 25,000 - 18,000 = an increase of Rs 7,000.

q: The Adjusted Profit and Loss Account of an enterprise shows the following items: balance of the profit and loss account at the commencement of the year Rs 60,000 (credit) and at the end of the year Rs 95,000 (credit); depreciation charged Rs 40,000; goodwill written off Rs 10,000; interim dividend paid Rs 25,000; amount transferred to the general reserve Rs 20,000; and a profit of Rs 15,000 on the sale of land credited to the profit and loss account. The funds from operations of the enterprise, being the balancing figure of the account, are:
e: Funds from operations = closing balance 95,000 - opening balance 60,000 + depreciation 40,000 + goodwill written off 10,000 + interim dividend 25,000 + transfer to general reserve 20,000 - profit on sale of land 15,000 = Rs 1,15,000.

q: During a year, an enterprise purchases plant for Rs 3,50,000 in cash and pays Rs 60,000 in cash for purchasing goodwill. It sells machinery for Rs 1,20,000 and long-term investments for Rs 80,000, and receives dividends of Rs 25,000 on its investments. Its net cash flow from investing activities is:

options.A: A net outflow of Rs 2,10,000
options.B: A net outflow of Rs 1,85,000
options.C: A net outflow of Rs 1,25,000
options.D: A net outflow of Rs 4,10,000

e: Investing outflows: plant 3,50,000 + goodwill 60,000 = 4,10,000. Investing inflows: machinery sold 1,20,000 + investments sold 80,000 + dividends received 25,000 = 2,25,000. Net cash flow = 2,25,000 - 4,10,000 = a net outflow of Rs 1,85,000.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise during a year is Rs 8,00,000. Its stock was Rs 90,000 at the commencement of the year and Rs 1,10,000 at the end of the year. Its trade creditors were Rs 75,000 at the commencement of the year and Rs 95,000 at the end of the year. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash paid to the suppliers during the year is:
e: Purchases = cost of goods sold 8,00,000 + closing stock 1,10,000 - opening stock 90,000 = 8,20,000. Cash paid to suppliers = purchases 8,20,000 + opening creditors 75,000 - closing creditors 95,000 = Rs 8,00,000.

q: The trade debtors of an enterprise were Rs 60,000 at the commencement of a year and Rs 85,000 at the end of the year. Its credit sales during the year were Rs 4,00,000. During the year, bad debts of Rs 10,000 were written off against the debtors and a discount of Rs 5,000 was allowed to them. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash received from the customers during the year is:
e: Cash received from customers = opening debtors 60,000 + credit sales 4,00,000 - closing debtors 85,000 - bad debts written off 10,000 - discount allowed 5,000 = Rs 3,60,000.

q: An enterprise has cash and cash equivalents of Rs 45,000 at the commencement of a year. During the year, its net cash flow from operating activities is an inflow of Rs 1,20,000, from investing activities an outflow of Rs 2,00,000 and from financing activities an inflow of Rs 95,000. Its cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year are:
e: Closing cash = opening 45,000 + operating inflow 1,20,000 - investing outflow 2,00,000 + financing inflow 95,000 = Rs 60,000.

q: In the cost ledger, the Stores Ledger Control Account shows an opening balance of Rs 1,20,000. During the period, materials purchased amounted to Rs 4,60,000, materials returned from production departments to the stores were Rs 25,000, materials issued to production were Rs 4,85,000 and materials returned to suppliers were Rs 15,000. The closing balance of the account is:
e: Closing Stores Ledger Control = opening 1,20,000 + purchases 4,60,000 + materials returned from production 25,000 - issues to production 4,85,000 - returns to suppliers 15,000 = Rs 1,05,000.

q: In a factory which maintains separate cost and financial books under the interlocking system, one account in the financial books summarises, in total, all the transactions entered in the cost books. That account is the:

options.A: General Ledger Adjustment Account
options.B: Stores Ledger Control Account
options.C: Cost Ledger Control Account
options.D: Memorandum Reconciliation Account

e: Under the interlocking system, the account in the financial books that summarises in total all transactions entered in the cost books is the Cost Ledger Control Account; the General Ledger Adjustment Account is its counterpart in the cost books.

q: The Work-in-Progress Ledger Control Account of a factory shows an opening balance of Rs 80,000. During the period, materials issued were Rs 3,20,000, direct wages accrued were Rs 1,80,000 and factory overheads absorbed were Rs 1,50,000. The closing work-in-progress is Rs 45,000. The cost of finished production transferred to the Finished Goods Ledger Control Account is:
e: Cost of finished production = opening WIP 80,000 + materials 3,20,000 + direct wages 1,80,000 + factory overheads absorbed 1,50,000 - closing WIP 45,000 = Rs 6,85,000.

q: Separable costs, in the costing of joint products, are those costs which:

options.A: Are incurred jointly before the split-off point and cannot be identified with individual products
options.B: Are apportioned among the joint products on the basis of their sales values
options.C: Represent the opportunity cost of the common facility used by all the products
options.D: Are incurred after the split-off point and can be identified wholly with an individual product

e: Separable costs are incurred after the split-off point and can be identified wholly with an individual product, unlike joint costs incurred before split-off which cannot be so identified.

q: A firm employs capital of Rs 50,00,000 in producing 1,00,000 units a year. The total cost of producing and selling this output is Rs 1,20,00,000. The firm fixes its selling price so as to earn a return of 16 per cent on the capital employed. The selling price per unit is:
e: Required profit = 16% x capital employed 50,00,000 = Rs 8,00,000. Total price = total cost 1,20,00,000 + 8,00,000 = 1,28,00,000, divided by 1,00,000 units = Rs 128.00 per unit.

q: Consider the following statements: 1. Joint products are produced from a common process and a common material and cannot be separated from one another until the split-off point is reached. 2. Co-products are produced simultaneously, generally by separate processes or from separate materials, and the proportion in which they are produced can be varied independently. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: Both 1 and 2
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements are correct: joint products come from a common process and material and cannot be separated until split-off, while co-products are produced simultaneously, generally by separate processes or materials, in proportions that can be varied independently.

q: After primary distribution, Service Department S1 has a total of Rs 75,000 and Service Department S2 a total of Rs 60,000. S1 renders service to S2 to the extent of 25 per cent of its work and S2 renders service to S1 to the extent of 25 per cent of its work. Under the reciprocal (simultaneous equation) method, the total cost of Service Department S1, after taking into account the service received from S2, is:
e: Let S1 and S2 be total costs after reciprocal services: S1 = 75,000 + 0.25 S2 and S2 = 60,000 + 0.25 S1. Substituting, S1 = 75,000 + 15,000 + 0.0625 S1, so 0.9375 S1 = 90,000 and S1 = Rs 96,000.

q: Consider the following statements about activity-based costing: 1. In the first stage, resource costs are assigned to activity cost pools by means of resource drivers. 2. In the second stage, the costs accumulated in the activity cost pools are assigned to products and other cost objects by means of activity drivers. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements describe ABC correctly: in stage one resource costs are assigned to activity cost pools using resource drivers, and in stage two pool costs are assigned to products and other cost objects using activity drivers.

q: The total factory overhead of a plant is Rs 9,00,000. On the basis of resource drivers, 20 per cent of this overhead is assigned to the machine set-up activity cost pool. During the period, 600 set-ups are performed in all, and one product requires 45 set-ups. The set-up cost assigned to that product is:
e: Set-up pool = 20% x 9,00,000 = Rs 1,80,000. Cost per set-up = 1,80,000 / 600 = Rs 300. Cost assigned to the product = 45 set-ups x 300 = Rs 13,500.

q: Merit rating of employees, as distinct from job evaluation, is the systematic assessment of:

options.A: The relative worth of an employee in terms of his qualities, performance and suitability for the work he is doing
options.B: The relative worth of a job in terms of its duties and responsibilities
options.C: The wage levels prevailing for a job in other organisations
options.D: The standard time that a qualified worker should take to perform a job

e: Merit rating assesses the employee himself - his qualities, performance and suitability for his work - whereas job evaluation assesses the relative worth of the job, not the person doing it.

q: A worker is paid for 48 hours in a week at Rs 75 per hour. His time booking for the week shows: time spent on jobs actually worked upon, 38 hours; normal idle time, 4 hours; abnormal idle time, 2 hours; and time spent on general maintenance work of the factory, 4 hours. The amount to be charged as direct labour cost to the jobs is:
e: Only time actually worked on jobs is direct labour: 38 hours x Rs 75 = Rs 2,850. Normal idle time goes to overhead, abnormal idle time to costing profit and loss, and general maintenance is indirect.

q: Job analysis, which forms the basis of job evaluation, consists of:

options.A: Fixing the wage rates to be paid for each grade of job in the factory
options.B: Comparing the output of one worker with that of another worker on the same job
options.C: Measuring the time taken by a worker to complete each element of a job
options.D: A detailed study and recording of the duties, responsibilities, working conditions and human requirements of a job

e: Job analysis is the detailed study and recording of a job's duties, responsibilities, working conditions and human requirements; it provides the job descriptions on which job evaluation is based.

q: The closing work-in-progress of a process is 3,000 units. The units are complete as regards materials but only 60 per cent complete as regards labour and overheads. The cost per equivalent unit is: materials Rs 12, labour Rs 8 and overheads Rs 5. The value of the closing work-in-progress is:
e: Closing WIP value: materials 3,000 units x 100% x Rs 12 = 36,000, labour 3,000 x 60% x Rs 8 = 14,400, overheads 3,000 x 60% x Rs 5 = 9,000; total = Rs 59,400.

q: Under Towne's gain-sharing plan of wage payment, the bonus paid to the workers is calculated as a share of:

options.A: The saving effected in the production cost of the work, as compared with a previously established standard cost
options.B: The time saved by the workers in completing their jobs, as in the Halsey plan
options.C: The increase in the output of the factory over the output of the previous year
options.D: The net profit earned by the enterprise during the year, divided among all employees

e: Under Towne's gain-sharing plan, workers share in the saving in production cost achieved against a previously established standard cost of the work, rather than in time saved or in total profit.

q: The Production Overhead Control Account of a factory is debited during a period with indirect materials of Rs 55,000, indirect wages of Rs 95,000 and indirect expenses of Rs 1,30,000. Overheads absorbed into work-in-progress during the period amount to Rs 2,95,000. The position at the end of the period is:

options.A: Under-absorption of Rs 15,000
options.B: Over-absorption of Rs 2,95,000
options.C: Under-absorption of Rs 2,80,000
options.D: Over-absorption of Rs 15,000

e: Actual overheads debited = 55,000 + 95,000 + 1,30,000 = Rs 2,80,000. Absorbed overheads are 2,95,000, which exceeds actual by 15,000, so there is over-absorption of Rs 15,000.

q: The principal object of codifying materials in a stores organisation — giving every item of material a distinct code number or symbol — is to:

options.A: Keep the existence of valuable items of stores secret from the storekeeper
options.B: Secure easy and unambiguous identification of each item and avoid duplication and long descriptive names
options.C: Enable the stores to be valued without reference to the price of the material
options.D: Fix the price at which the material will be issued to production

e: Codification gives every material item a distinct code number or symbol so each item is easily and unambiguously identified, avoiding duplication and long descriptive names.

q: The total lighting cost of a factory for a period is Rs 48,000, and it is apportioned among the departments on the basis of the number of light points in each department. Department X has 120 light points, Department Y has 80 and Department Z has 40. The share of the lighting cost borne by Department X is:
e: Total light points = 120 + 80 + 40 = 240. Department X share = 120/240 x Rs 48,000 = Rs 24,000.

q: Group technology, applied in organising production in a factory, is based on the principle of:

options.A: Grouping components and parts into families according to the similarity of their design and processing requirements, so that each family can be produced in a dedicated cell of machines
options.B: Grouping all machines of the same type together in a single department, through which every job must pass
options.C: Producing the entire requirement of every component in one single large batch at the beginning of the year
options.D: Arranging the products of the firm in groups according to their selling prices for the purpose of fixing overhead rates

e: Group technology groups components into families by similarity of design and processing requirements, so each family can be produced in a dedicated machine cell, reducing set-ups and movement.

q: Factory overheads are absorbed at 25 per cent of the prime cost. The works cost of a job is Rs 9,00,000. The prime cost of the job is:
e: Works cost = prime cost + 25% of prime cost = 1.25 x prime cost. So prime cost = 9,00,000 / 1.25 = Rs 7,20,000.

q: A material transfer note is used in a factory when:

options.A: Material is issued from the stores to a production department against a requisition
options.B: Material is transferred directly from one job or department to another, without being returned to the stores
options.C: Material received from a supplier is sent for inspection before acceptance
options.D: Surplus material lying with a department is returned to the stores for safe custody

e: A material transfer note records material transferred directly from one job or department to another without being returned to stores; issues from stores use a requisition and returns to stores use a material return note.
